sentences.t: Policybazaar was founded in June 2008 by Yashish Dahiya, Alok Bansal and Avaneesh Nirjar (Wikipedia and Founder Nation agree on the date and the names).
Dahiya had studied at IIT Delhi and IIM Ahmedabad, then INSEAD, worked at Bain and then at the online travel business ebookers.
Forbes India quotes him in 2017 saying that the idea of becoming an aggregator emerged from ebookers.
That is the core of the model: in travel, a site lists every airline's price and the customer chooses.
That is the model it applied to insurance.
Early money came from Info Edge, the company behind Naukri.
The amount is where sources split.
Forbes India's 2018 profile says ₹20 crore.
Wikipedia says ₹30 million, which is ₹3 crore.
These cannot both be right, and I could not find a primary source, so I am not giving a figure.
Intel Capital invested in 2011.
A second conflict is when co-founder Nirjar left.
Forbes in 2017 and Founder Nation say 2011.
Forbes in 2018 says 2013.
I have not resolved it.
Dahiya told Forbes in 2017 that insurers went to the regulator to "kill us".
One reason, in the same coverage, was that Policybazaar's selling point was transparency: it showed customers what a policy cost and what the commissions were.
For an industry whose sales ran through agents, a site that lined up products side by side threatened the usual way of selling.
The company survived, and the regulator eventually licensed web aggregators as a category.
A web-aggregator licence existed, since Policybazaar surrendered one in 2021.
Forbes India's 2018 profile says the aggregator business turned profitable in FY2016-17.
At that time online insurance was about 5% of the Indian market, and Policybazaar had about half of that.
In June 2018 a round led by SoftBank put in $238 million.
Forbes breaks that into $200 million of new capital and $38 million bought from existing holders.
Info Edge's share of that deal was $58 million.
Tencent invested in 2019.
The same profile shows how the company actually sold.
Customers filled in a form online, then the call centre did the work: about 2 lakh voice calls a day, with speech analytics on the recordings, and around 75% of conversations in Hindi.
The website was the lead source, and the phone was the sales channel.
That detail matters for anyone who thinks online insurance means self-service.
In India it largely meant online lead generation and human selling.
The company also launched DocPrime, a doctor-booking service, in the same period.
PB Fintech went public on 15 November 2021 and raised ₹5,625 crore.
Earlier that year, in June 2021, the company obtained a broking licence, surrendered its web-aggregator licence and began opening offline outlets.
In plain terms, it stopped being only a comparison site.
As a broker it can advise and place business and be paid commissions, with different rules from an aggregator.
Fortune India reported on 5 August 2026 for the first quarter of FY27.
Revenue was ₹1,888 crore, up 40.1%.
Profit after tax was ₹163 crore, up 92.4%.
Total premium sold was ₹8,372 crore, up 41%.
Core insurance renewal revenue was running at an annualised rate (ARR) of ₹999 crore, a run rate and not revenue earned in the quarter.
The platform had sold 7.16 crore policies to 2.81 crore customers.
Its profit margin moved from minus 47% in the June 2021 quarter to plus 9% now.
I am leaving out full-year FY26 profit growth because two sources give 90% and 115%.
Wikipedia lists three events.
In May 2021 the insurance regulator fined the company ₹2.4 million.
In July 2022 there was a data breach.
In January 2025 there was a GST raid.
I have not read primary documents on any of them, so these are listed as reported and not assessed.
Pick a customer pain the industry hides.
Showing prices and commissions made the product popular with buyers and unpopular with insurers.
This is supported by Dahiya's own account.
Online demand, human closing.
The 2 lakh daily calls show that in complex, low-frequency products, the website finds the customer and a person completes the sale.
This is my reading of the Forbes figures.
Renewals are the quiet engine.
Renewal revenue, running at an annualised ₹999 crore per Fortune India, is the part that compounds, though I do not have the same figure for earlier years to show the trend.
Regulation is part of the business.
The company moved from aggregator to broker in 2021.
Today it faces IRDAI's draft commission caps, whose feedback window closes 25 October.
Why it matters this weekThe draft proposes lower commissions on health, motor and credit-linked insurance.
ICRA expects the effect in FY28.
I do not know how much of PB Fintech's revenue comes from the product lines affected, so I will not guess its exposure.
